label: General MIDI standard drum kit, close mics, dry
audition_title: libsonare drum kit vs the sampled reference
_channel: Channel 10 (9 zero-based) is what makes a note number select an instrument instead of a pitch, on the reference as much as in libsonare. A drum sampler that answers on any channel will still record correctly here; a GM-conformant reference will record a piano if this is left off, and the corpus would look like a successful capture of the wrong instrument.
_dry: Close mics with the plugin's room and bus sections off. A kit is the one percussion case where dry is both achievable and wanted: the ambience is a mix decision rather than part of the instrument, and libsonare's own send weighting is fitted separately. If the reference cannot be dried - some kits bake the overheads into every sample - clear `dry` and let the room correction handle it, the same way the organ capture does. Here it was achieved: `calibrate` measures RT60 0.00 s, against 3.14 s on the organ capture, so the switch reached what it advertised.
_calibration: From `capture.py calibrate`: the reference renders identically in real time and faster than it, and the measured settle minimum is 250 ms. `realtime` is on anyway, and the reason is a measurement rather than caution. Rendering this grid with it off failed 63 of 282 notes - the sampler returned digital silence and the retry found it five times running - and the failures were not the exotic notes but the snare, the closed hi-hat and the ride. So `calibrate` measuring real time as optional says only that one note on an otherwise idle machine did not need it; a 282-note grid streaming from disk, on a machine doing anything else at the same time, does. Read that recipe line as the floor it is.
_stimulus: 50 ms, because on a drum channel the note-off carries no information: a kit's percussion is voiced as a one-shot and renders identically at any gate. Measured rather than assumed, on the three notes that would show a choke first - open hi-hat, ride and crash, rendered at 50, 250 and 1000 ms - and the RMS agrees to inside 0.1 dB in every window out to two seconds. Worth measuring because the failure is silent: a kit that did choke would fill the corpus with short cymbals and nothing downstream would report anything but a successful capture. The remaining exceptions are the notes a kit voices as held instruments - typically the whistles and the record scratches - whose length is whatever the gate was on the reference side and a constant on the model side. Fitting one of those means re-capturing it at a longer gate, not reading its envelope from this grid.
_round_robin: A sampled kit commonly alternates between several recordings of the same strike, which makes the reference non-deterministic in a way that reads as measurement noise in every metric. `capture.py calibrate` renders the same note twice and reports whether the two agree; check that before trusting a corpus, because a round robin left on puts a floor under the loss that no knob can go below. On this capture the two renders are bit-identical, so there is no such floor and a loss that stops falling has stopped for a reason worth finding.
_timbres: One kit per timbre, on its own channel slot if the plugin is a rack.
_notes: The General MIDI standard kit, note 35 to note 81, every instrument in it. A drum fit is per-note - each instrument is its own patch, or shares one with its neighbours - so there is no register to interpolate across and no note that another note stands in for.
_toms: The six tom keys do NOT hold the pitch order General MIDI names them in, so a tom fit scored against this capture note-for-note fits the wrong drum. Measured fundamentals, consistent across velocities 64/100/127: note 45 at 67-73 Hz, 47 at 73-83, 48 at 87-93, 50 at 93-97, 41 at 163-170, 43 at 183-190. That is a clean ascending series of six toms laid out as 45, 47, 48, 50, 41, 43 - the two smallest toms sit on the low-floor-tom keys, where GM puts the two largest. libsonare's own toms key-track, so they run 100 to 167 Hz in note order and no single key pairs with its reference row: 41 and 43 read 0.6x the reference and 45 through 50 read 1.6-1.9x. Every other family in this capture does follow GM - the hats, snares and cymbals were identified by their band profiles and fitted against these rows - so this is a property of the six tom keys and not of the capture. Nothing here is wrong as a measurement; the rows are correct for the keys they were struck on. What is blocked is reading a tom disagreement as a voicing error.
_bandwidth: This capture measures nothing above roughly 6 kHz, and what it reports there is its own upper edge rather than the kit's. Every instrument in it collapses at the same rate: taken relative to their own loudest band, a crash, a cowbell, a closed hi-hat and a cabasa agree to within a few dB from 6.3 kHz upward while differing by 7-8 dB at 4 kHz, which four different objects cannot do and one shared transfer function must. The crash reads -25.1 dB at 6.3 kHz, -34.4 at 8, -55.9 at 10.1, -86.6 at 12.7 and -122.3 at 16 - past 100 dB per octave and accelerating, where a real cymbal is still radiating. It belongs to this reference rather than to the harness: through the same path the organ capture reads -61 dB at 16 kHz, the harpsichord -48, and libsonare's own render -0.1. In the measurement it surfaces as a floor - 276 of the 282 rows sit exactly on the band floor at 12.5 kHz and the loudest row in the whole kit reaches only -56.7 - so a model with any energy up there is scored against a wall it should not be asked to reproduce. The metric does not yet know this: 20 % of the band-profile objective, and 46 % of it on the vibraslap, is summed above 6.3 kHz, where 599 of those 1128 reference bands are on the floor. Read a top-octave excess as unmeasured rather than as too bright, and fit the low and mid bands, which are sound.
_velocities: Velocity is the only axis a drum note has, so the grid carries both the set a fit is scored on (64, 100, 127) and the set it is validated against (48, 88, 112) from the same capture. Rendering the holdout now is what makes the generalisation check free later; capturing only the fit set makes it impossible.
_dimensions: Empty means all of them, and here that is a decision rather than a default. A kit gets the percussion dimensions - band tilt, band profile error, per-octave decay, attack, crest, brightness and velocity range - because the pitched ones are built on a fundamental (the harmonic ladder, the intonation error, the tone-to-noise ratio) and a drum hit does not have one. Which of them a gate can hold was measured rather than judged: for each dimension, the spread of the delta across the six velocities of one instrument against the spread across the 47 instruments. A dimension where the first approaches the second is measuring the measurement, and none of these do - the ratios run 0.12 to 0.37. Per-octave decay reads 0.25 despite swinging by hundreds of dB/s within single notes near the top of the kit, which is why it is in rather than out: the swing is a handful of instruments, not the dimension.
_identity: Which product this is captured from lives in the untracked sibling `drums.local.json`: the plugin's component triple and each timbre's preset. Everything here is the method. Re-capturing needs the overlay; scoring and fitting read the rendered corpus and need nothing.
